sections.rule: One correct option. One mark each. No negative marking.
Enter the final figure only. No marks for working.
Match every pair. Two marks each. All or nothing.

paper.caselet: A meal programme cooks 90,000 portions from one kitchen each morning and must deliver to 480 schools before 12:30. Cooking finishes at 07:30. Its 42 vehicles average 11 schools each per run, and last month 26 schools received meals after 12:30 on at least four days.
paper.stem: Where is the constraint on this operation?
options: In the distribution window between 07:30 and 12:30, since cooking is already complete before dispatch begins
In the number of schools, since 480 destinations is more than 42 vehicles can reasonably serve
In kitchen capacity, since 90,000 portions from one kitchen is the largest number in the case and scale of that order is what limits any operation
In the vehicles, since more of them would remove the late deliveries directly and additional capacity is the fastest route to serving the whole list on time

paper.caselet: A appliance maker promises next-day delivery on a range it has just widened from 40 to 260 variants, while keeping its existing quarterly production runs, single central warehouse and cheapest-quote carrier contracts.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible reading?
options: The carrier contract is the weak link, and re-tendering it will deliver the promise, since the days are lost in transit rather than before it
The wider range is the problem on its own, and cutting variants back to 40 restores the position without touching the production runs or the warehouse
The promise and the operating design now describe different businesses, so one of the two has to move
Nothing needs to change, because demand variability has not risen and the forecast is unchanged, and the uncertainty a chain absorbs is a property of its customers

paper.caselet: A state wants to raise container throughput at a public port. Average vessel turnaround is 2.4 days against 0.9 at a nearby private terminal; the public port's cranes are older and its yard is congested, and the state has limited capital to invest.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible route?
options: Fund new cranes from the state budget, because ownership must stay entirely public for a strategic asset whatever the capital constraint the state is working under
Bring in private capital and operating discipline for the terminal while the state keeps the port's public role
Sell the port outright, since the private terminal already performs better on turnaround and ownership is what produced that difference
Accept the difference, because turnaround is decided by vessel size and cargo mix rather than by operations, so equipment and yard management cannot close it

paper.caselet: A planner has used a smoothing constant of 0.1 for two years. A competitor's exit has permanently lifted weekly demand, and for six weeks the forecast has sat well below actual demand every week.
paper.stem: What should the planner do?
options: Switch to using last week's actual demand as next week's forecast until the gap closes, since the most recent figure is the best available estimate of the new level
Raise the constant so the forecast catches the level shift, accepting that it will also track noise more closely
Keep the constant, because a low value is what protects a forecast from over-reacting, and that protection is worth more than a faster response to any single run
Leave the method alone, since six weeks of error is normal variation around a forecast and reacting to a short run is how planners end up chasing noise

paper.caselet: A buyer is told the supplier has cut the fixed charge per order from ₹4,000 to ₹1,000. Annual demand and holding cost are unchanged.
paper.stem: What should happen to the order quantity, and why?
options: It should not change, because the order quantity is set by annual demand, which the supplier's charge does not affect in either direction
It should fall to a quarter, because the ordering cost has fallen to a quarter
It should fall to half, because the quantity moves with the square root of the ordering cost
It should rise, because cheaper ordering makes larger orders more attractive and the saving is best captured by buying in bulk

paper.caselet: A bakery makes a celebration cake for one weekend only. Each sells for ₹1,200 and costs ₹400 to make. Anything unsold is given away at the end of the weekend and returns nothing.
paper.stem: What does this cost structure imply about the quantity to bake?
options: Bake exactly expected demand, since that is the quantity which minimises the total mismatch cost on either side
Bake well above expected demand, because a missed sale costs twice what an unsold cake does
Bake below expected demand, because unsold stock returns nothing at all and a zero salvage value is the strongest argument for caution
The quantity cannot be decided without knowing how many were sold last year, since the costs alone cannot indicate a quantity

paper.caselet: Moving a consignment by road costs ₹210,000 and takes 4 days. By rail and coastal shipping combined it costs ₹96,000 and takes 13 days. The consignment is a spare part held as insurance stock against a breakdown that halts a ₹40 lakh-a-day production line.
paper.stem: Which mode should be chosen, and on what basis?
options: Rail and coastal, because it is less than half the freight cost and the saving is certain while the breakdown it guards against may never happen at all
Road, because the nine days saved are worth far more than the ₹114,000 difference given what a stoppage costs
Rail and coastal, because slower modes are the correct default for heavy or bulky consignments
Either, since freight cost is the only figure that separates two modes carrying the same goods to the same destination in the same condition

paper.caselet: A firm sited four stockyards when road freight cost ₹4 per tonne-km and each yard could serve a 90 km radius economically. Freight is now ₹9 per tonne-km, the economic radius has fallen to about 55 km, and demand has grown in two districts that sit at the edge of two existing yards.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible response?
options: Close the two least-used yards, since higher freight cost makes fewer, larger sites cheaper to run and consolidation is the standard response to dearer transport
Keep the sites, because a stockyard is a long-lived asset and moving it destroys the investment already committed to building and equipping it
Add a yard in each of the two growing districts and leave the existing four unchanged
Re-run the siting decision on the new cost, radius and demand together, since all three inputs have changed

paper.caselet: End-customer sales of a household product have varied by about 5% month to month for two years. Retailer orders to the distributor vary by 20%, distributor orders to the manufacturer by 45%, and the manufacturer's production schedule by 70%.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible interpretation?
options: End demand must be more variable than the sales figures show, since orders reflect it and a 70% swing could not arise from demand varying by 5%
The manufacturer's planning is at fault, since its swing is the largest of the four and the biggest number in a chain marks where the problem is created
Each stage is adding distortion by ordering from the stage in front of it rather than from real demand
The pattern is expected, because orders further from the customer are naturally less accurate

paper.caselet: A firm's order-to-delivery time is 19 days. Measured stage by stage, actual work accounts for about 3 days; the rest is orders waiting for the next batch run, for credit approval, and for a weekly despatch window.
paper.stem: Where should the redesign start?
options: With the three days of actual work, because that is the part the firm directly controls
With the waiting between stages, since that is where sixteen of the nineteen days are
With the despatch window alone, since it is the last delay before the customer and therefore the one they actually experience
With adding capacity at each stage, so that work is completed faster everywhere

paper.caselet: A firm sources two components from one low-cost offshore supplier: a stable, high-volume fastener, and a fast-changing electronic module whose design revises every few months and whose demand swings sharply.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible sourcing change?
options: Keep the fastener offshore and move the module to a responsive supplier nearer the market
Keep both offshore, because the cost advantage applies to everything the firm buys, whatever the design revision rate or the demand pattern of the part
Move both to the responsive supplier, since a single relationship is simpler to manage and the coordination saved outweighs the premium paid on the stable part
Move both onshore, because offshore sourcing carries disruption risk in every category, and that exposure settles the question ahead of any cost comparison

paper.caselet: Sales forecasts 40,000 units for the quarter, operations has capacity for 28,000 and plans to that, and finance has budgeted revenue on 36,000. Each number is circulated separately and none is reconciled before the quarter starts.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible reading?
options: Operations should build to 40,000, because the plan must serve whatever sales can sell
Three functions are committing the firm to three different quarters, and the reconciliation is the missing step
Sales should reduce its forecast to 28,000, since capacity is the hard limit and the rest is aspiration
The spread is acceptable because a forecast is uncertain and each function needs its own working figure

paper.caselet: A cold-store owner runs at 95% occupancy for four months of the year and 30% for the other eight. A neighbouring plot is available. Adding a chamber would cost ₹1.4 crore, and the additional produce is available only in the same four-month window.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible reading?
options: The new chamber would be idle for eight months, so its case rests on what the peak four months alone can cover
Occupancy averages about 52% across the year, so there is spare capacity and no case for building until the annual average approaches the physical limit of the site
The expansion is justified, because turning away produce in the peak is a lost sale
The plot should be bought regardless, since land beside an existing site rarely becomes available twice and the option is worth more than the analysis that would delay it

paper.caselet: A retailer wants to cut delivery time to stores. It is considering three options: adding two regional warehouses, moving a third of volume from rail to road, or raising the safety stock held at the existing single warehouse.
paper.stem: Which reading of these three options is correct?
options: Whichever of the three drivers costs least should be chosen, since each reaches the same delivery time and the decision is purely a question of price
These are three drivers of one outcome, but facilities is what counts, since delivery time is set by where stock sits
Transportation is always the best of these drivers, because moving faster is the only real lever on time
They are three different drivers of the same outcome, and the choice is a cost trade rather than a ranking

paper.caselet: A fleet operator pays drivers a fixed sum per trip. Average round-trip time is 46 hours, of which 19 are spent waiting to load and unload. The operator is considering buying four more trucks to raise the number of trips completed each week.
paper.stem: What should be examined before the purchase?
options: Whether the drivers can be paid more per trip, since faster driving would shorten the round trip
Whether removing part of the 19 waiting hours would raise trips per truck without buying anything
Whether four trucks is the right number, given that the fleet is the binding constraint
Whether fuel cost per trip can be reduced, since that is the largest variable cost of a round trip

paper.caselet: A state has risen four places in the national logistics ranking. Its industry association reports that road quality and warehousing availability scores improved, while its members' own freight costs and delivery times are unchanged.
paper.stem: What is the most defensible reading?
options: The improvement proves logistics performance has risen, and firms will be reporting savings shortly, since better roads and warehousing pass through to costs automatically
The ranking must be wrong, because the outcome that matters to firms has not moved, and a measure that does not track members' freight costs is measuring nothing useful
The index measures firm-level outcomes directly, so the two findings cannot both be true and one of the two reports has to be withdrawn
The index measures the environment a supply chain operates in, so a better score need not yet show in firms' own costs

paper.caselet: An apparel brand's warehouses and stores are already built and a festive peak is eight weeks away, so a team must settle how much stock to position where and how much output to subcontract.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Decision phases: Reopen the warehouse locations, since a demand peak is the moment to reconsider where the network's fixed assets should sit.
Decision phases: Wait for the actual orders, because a decision made before demand is known belongs to operations and cannot be taken any earlier than that.
Decision phases: Treat the subcontracting question as a design commitment and evaluate it over a multi-year horizon.

Decision phases: Handle it as supply chain planning: hold the network fixed and set inventory, production and subcontracting policies across the horizon, because the design questions were already answered.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Ports and PPP is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Ports and PPP to the wider subject?
options: Ports and PPP improves one local measure, so effects elsewhere in the system stop mattering.
Ports and PPP works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Once Ports and PPP has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.
A port is a transfer node, so capacity creates trade value only when sea-side operations and inland flows work together.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Supply chain surplus is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Supply chain surplus to the wider subject?
options: Only the customer pays into the chain, so a local gain that raises total cost shrinks the pie everyone shares.
Supply chain surplus works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Supply chain surplus improves one local measure, so effects elsewhere in the system stop mattering.
Once Supply chain surplus has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.

paper.caselet: A terminal adds modern handling capacity, but road and rail evacuation remain congested and ships still face delays.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Ports and PPP: Measure port capability by total national coastline length rather than by cargo actually moved.
Ports and PPP: Treat terminal investment, hinterland connectivity and service as one system, since capacity pays only when both sides work.
Ports and PPP: Declare the port problem fixed because the cranes are newer than the ones they replaced.
Ports and PPP: Remove performance oversight once private investment is committed, since the operator now carries the commercial risk.

paper.caselet: A state ranks poorly on tracking, infrastructure, regulatory environment, and cargo safety in stakeholder surveys.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: LEADS index: Use the dimensions to target state policy, remembering the measure is perception-based and never a guarantee of firm performance.
LEADS index: Improve only warehouse capacity, because infrastructure, regulation, tracking, and cargo safety are not what the index reads.
LEADS index: Ignore the stakeholder evidence entirely, since perception surveys cannot indicate anything about how a state's logistics actually performs.
LEADS index: Treat the state's rank as a firm-level profit statement and plan individual company budgets from it.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Inventory functions and measures is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Inventory functions and measures to the wider subject?
options: Stock is held for a reason, so how fast it moves means little until that reason is named.
Once Inventory functions and measures has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.
Inventory functions and measures improves one local measure, so effects elsewhere in the system stop mattering.
Inventory functions and measures works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.

paper.caselet: An assembly line runs at sixty units an hour and a unit takes ten hours from entry to exit. Management wants average inventory in the system halved without losing throughput.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Logistical drivers: Cut order quantities until stock reaches three hundred units, since inventory is what the instruction named and lot size is what sets it.
Logistical drivers: Raise throughput to a hundred and twenty units an hour so the same ten-hour flow time yields the lower inventory figure the instruction asked for.
Logistical drivers: Read the target through Little's Law: with throughput held, halving inventory to three hundred units is an instruction to halve flow time to five hours.
Logistical drivers: Declare the target unreachable, because flow time is a property of the process and only capital investment can change it.

paper.caselet: A retailer facing an uncertain season orders well below what would maximise the chain's profit, because unsold units are written off entirely at its own cost.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Risk-sharing contracts: Cut the wholesale price until the retailer orders more, treating the order quantity as a pure function of margin.
Risk-sharing contracts: Adopt revenue sharing without any means of verifying reported sales, because a contract that lowers the wholesale price gives the supplier enough protection on its own.
Risk-sharing contracts: Require the retailer to commit to the chain-optimal quantity outright, since the number itself is what the contract needs to specify.
Risk-sharing contracts: Use a buyback or revenue-sharing term so the supplier carries part of the leftover risk, and expect the retailer's order to rise toward the chain-optimal quantity.

paper.caselet: A fashion item has one buying opportunity, uncertain seasonal demand, and heavy markdowns after the season.
paper.stem: Which model fits best and why?
options: A Q review model, because replenishment can occur continuously at any point after the season starts.
Exponential smoothing alone, because updating the forecast directly chooses the profit-maximising order quantity.
EOQ, because demand is constant across the year and replenishment orders repeat indefinitely.
Newsvendor, because a one-time uncertain order turns on shortage and leftover costs.

paper.caselet: Retail sales move slightly, but retailer, wholesaler, and manufacturer orders show progressively larger peaks and troughs.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Bullwhip effect: Assume consumer demand moved by the same amount, and read the manufacturer's order swings as a true demand signal.
Bullwhip effect: Add more safety stock at every stage without addressing the order distortion that created the swings, since buffering is what inventory is there to do.
Bullwhip effect: Diagnose amplification across incentives, batching, forecast updates and lead times, since only a shared demand signal stops it.
Bullwhip effect: Ask each stage to optimise its own profit without sharing demand data, since local accountability serves the chain best.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Cold-storage expansion?
options: Cold-storage expansion: Cold-storage expansion must be judged through seasonal utilisation, commodity flows, operating cost, financing, and market relationships—not capacity alone.
Cold-storage expansion: Cold storage earns the same return at every utilisation level, since its costs rise and fall with the volume stored.
Cold-storage expansion: Debt structure and seasonal demand do not affect expansion risk once the facility is technically sound and well run.
Cold-storage expansion: A profitable existing site proves any new geography will work, because the operating model travels with the operator.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Total cost of ownership and aggregation?
options: Total cost of ownership and aggregation: Total cost of ownership is the purchase price plus freight, since everything after delivery belongs to operations rather than to the sourcing decision.

Total cost of ownership and aggregation: A third-party provider is cheaper only where it pays lower wages, so a firm with the same labour rates can always match it by doing the work itself, since aggregation across many clients cannot create a cost advantage on its own.
Total cost of ownership and aggregation: Aggregation only reduces cost when the pooled volumes are identical, because a third party cannot smooth variability across clients whose demand differs.

Total cost of ownership and aggregation: Total cost of ownership adds freight, inventory, quality, and coordination to the purchase price, and a third party earns its margin by aggregation — pooling capacity, inventory, transport or procurement across many clients.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Qualitative and quantitative forecasting is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Qualitative and quantitative forecasting to the wider subject?
options: Method choice follows what the data can support, so a product with no history is not forecast the way a mature one is.
Qualitative and quantitative forecasting improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Once Qualitative and quantitative forecasting has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Qualitative and quantitative forecasting works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.

paper.stem: What raises the implied demand uncertainty a supply chain has to absorb?
options: It rises when suppliers are chosen on price rather than on reliability, and falls again when they are not.
Only the variability of the underlying demand raises it, since the promise made about it is a marketing matter.
Nothing raises it except a forecast error large enough to cause a stockout in the current period.
Shorter lead times, wider variety, more channels, higher service levels and faster innovation all raise it.

paper.caselet: Sea freight is far cheaper per tonne than rail but arrives in one very large annual lot and requires port, barge, and inland handling.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Multimodal cost trade-off: Choose sea immediately on the line-haul rate per tonne, since the gap against rail is too large to be reversed.
Multimodal cost trade-off: Exclude port, barge, and inland handling from both options, comparing only the long-haul movement between them.
Multimodal cost trade-off: Compare movement cost plus inventory and handling before choosing sea, because the freight rate never decides a mode by itself.
Multimodal cost trade-off: Choose rail because it moves smaller consignments, without costing the inventory that each shipment size creates.

paper.caselet: Secondary delivery becomes more expensive than primary line-haul and dealers require an overnight service radius.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Stockyard location trade-off: Keep the existing sites, because demand locations alone determine where a stockyard belongs, whatever has since changed in transport cost or coverage limit.
Stockyard location trade-off: Re-evaluate site locations using the changed cost structure, coverage limit, demand, and minimum throughput together.
Stockyard location trade-off: Consolidate into one large site regardless of dealer distance, since fewer sites always mean lower total network cost.
Stockyard location trade-off: Minimise primary line-haul distance while leaving secondary delivery cost out of the comparison entirely.

paper.caselet: A loaded rake waits an average 13 hours for a locomotive, limiting monthly trips despite adequate loading capacity.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Transport turnaround: Buy additional rakes before addressing the 13-hour wait, since more assets must produce more trips.
Transport turnaround: Coordinate an engine-on-load arrangement and accountability for the hand-off so detention falls and trips per rake rise.
Transport turnaround: Measure only tonnes loaded per wagon and ignore cycle time, since a fuller wagon is always a more productive one.
Transport turnaround: Increase factory output while loaded wagons continue to stand idle, because production volume is what limits despatch.

paper.caselet: A rake cycle of 99 hours breaks down as loading 3.5 hours, idle before loading 7.5, waiting for a locomotive after loading 13, transit out 34, transit back 30, and unloading and readying about 9.75.
paper.stem: Which element is the largest single inefficiency to attack, as opposed to the largest block of time?
options: Transit out at 34 hours, which is the largest element in the cycle and therefore the biggest prize.
Waiting for a locomotive at 13 hours, which is detention created by the engine being reassigned elsewhere.
Idle time before loading at 7.5 hours, which is pure waiting and adds nothing to the movement.
Unloading and readying at about 9.75 hours, which is the element most directly under the plant's control.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Supply-chain re-engineering?
options: Supply-chain re-engineering: It means cutting one department's budget without examining the stages upstream and downstream of it.
Supply-chain re-engineering: Customer segments should receive identical logistics regardless of need, since one uniform service level is simplest to run and audit.
Supply-chain re-engineering: More inventory is the default answer to every service problem, because stock is what protects a customer from delay.
Supply-chain re-engineering: Re-engineering redesigns end-to-end flows to remove hidden time, inventory, hand-offs, and cost while meeting distinct customer service needs.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Demand components and forecast error is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Demand components and forecast error to the wider subject?
options: Demand components and forecast error improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system can be treated as somebody else's problem to solve later on.
Demand components and forecast error works in exactly the same way regardless of the people involved, the constraints in force, and the decisions being taken around it at the time.
Which pattern the data carries decides which method fits, and the error left over is what sets the buffer, so measuring it is planning rather than reporting.
Once Demand components and forecast error has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen it, because a decision that keeps moving is not really a decision.

paper.caselet: A plant with costly hiring and training faces seasonal demand, while its product can be stored economically.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Sales and operations planning: Use a level plan and draw inventory down, since a forecast becomes a decision only when reconciled with capacity cost.
Sales and operations planning: Ignore the forecast until daily orders arrive, because only confirmed orders justify committing capacity.
Sales and operations planning: Absorb the whole peak with backlog even where customers will not tolerate delay, since backlog costs nothing to hold.
Sales and operations planning: Hire and release workers to match each monthly demand change exactly, since matching output to demand avoids holding inventory.

paper.caselet: A retailer promises low prices and dependable availability but keeps many premium express facilities with duplicated stock.
paper.stem: Which diagnosis is best?
options: More facilities always improve both efficiency and responsiveness at the same time, so the network is already configured correctly for any promise.
Its facilities and inventory choices may be more responsive—and costly—than the competitive promise requires, so the driver configuration lacks strategic fit.
The only useful response is to add more product variety, since a wider range is what a low-price promise needs.
Pricing and supply-chain choices are unrelated, because price is set in the market while cost is settled inside operations.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Modes and national logistics reforms?
options: Modes and national logistics reforms: Dedicated freight corridors raise speed by adding track for passenger services, freeing the existing lines for freight to share as before, so a container train on a corridor still waits behind scheduled passenger services at every junction along its route to the port.

Modes and national logistics reforms: Multimodal transport means using several carriers within one mode, so a consignment handed between two trucking firms has moved multimodally, while the same consignment moving by rail and then by road has stayed inside a single mode throughout its journey and needs no transfer arrangement.

Modes and national logistics reforms: PM Gati Shakti is a freight tracking system for consignments in transit, which is what separates it from a platform for planning infrastructure, so a ministry deciding where a new road or terminal should go consults it only after construction has finished and traffic has begun to move over it.

Modes and national logistics reforms: Multimodal transport moves one consignment across road, rail, sea or air, and India's reforms — dedicated freight corridors, PM Gati Shakti, the Unified Logistics Interface Platform and the landlord port model — attack speed, planning, visibility and port operation.

paper.caselet: A consignment currently moves entirely by road. Rail would be cheaper per tonne over the long leg, but the goods still need collection at origin and delivery at destination.
paper.stem: What is the best interpretation or next step?
options: Modes and national logistics reforms: Rule rail out because it cannot reach either end, treating a mode that needs a transfer as unusable for this consignment.
Modes and national logistics reforms: Plan it as a multimodal movement and cost the two handling transfers alongside the line-haul saving, since the rail leg cannot serve either end by itself.
Modes and national logistics reforms: Assume a dedicated freight corridor removes the transfers, since undisturbed running is what makes the rail leg competitive in the first place.
Modes and national logistics reforms: Compare the road and rail rates per tonne and choose the lower, because the long leg is where nearly all the distance sits.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Features of a good forecast is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Features of a good forecast to the wider subject?
options: Once Features of a good forecast has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen or change the decision.
Features of a good forecast works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Features of a good forecast improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
A forecast is useful only where its horizon, its units and its stated error fit the decision waiting on it.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Ecosystem actors and shipper decisions?
options: Ecosystem actors and shipper decisions: The macro ecosystem actors are shippers, the industry, infrastructure and service providers, and government, and shipper decision horizons sort a brand owner's choices into strategic, tactical and operational bands.
Ecosystem actors and shipper decisions: Government enters only as a regulator, so its role in envisioning, developing and enabling infrastructure belongs to the service providers instead.
Ecosystem actors and shipper decisions: A shipper is the transport company that carries the goods, and the brand owner appears in the ecosystem only as its customer.
Ecosystem actors and shipper decisions: Industry-level action is the sum of what individual shippers already do, which is why nothing changes when firms with similar attributes coordinate.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Six supply-chain drivers?
options: Six supply-chain drivers: Transportation speed alone determines supply-chain performance, because every other driver follows the delivery schedule.
Six supply-chain drivers: Each driver can be optimised independently, so the best network is the sum of six separate local optima.
Six supply-chain drivers: Adding facilities always lowers both total cost and total inventory, since local stock is cheaper to hold.
Six supply-chain drivers: Facilities, inventory, transportation, information, sourcing, and pricing jointly set the balance between responsiveness and efficiency.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Six supply-chain drivers is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Six supply-chain drivers to the wider subject?
options: Managers deliver strategic fit by configuring several connected drivers, not by maximising one lever in isolation.
Six supply-chain drivers improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system no longer matters here at all.
Once Six supply-chain drivers has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.
Six supply-chain drivers works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Financial measures of a supply chain is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Financial measures of a supply chain to the wider subject?
options: Financial measures of a supply chain works independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions around it.
Financial measures of a supply chain improves one local measure, so effects elsewhere in the system stop mattering.
Margins, stock and payment timing are where operating choices land, so a supply chain decision is traceable to the number it moves.
Once Financial measures of a supply chain has settled the choice, later evidence should not change the decision.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Tailored sourcing portfolio?
options: Tailored sourcing portfolio: Innovative products with short lives must always be sourced fully offshore, since low labour cost matters most where margins are thin.

Tailored sourcing portfolio: A sourcing portfolio matches responsive sources to volatile, high-value or time-sensitive items and efficient sources to stable, predictable volume while managing disruption risk.
Tailored sourcing portfolio: Nearshoring removes every cost and disruption trade-off at once, so a closer supplier needs no comparison against a cheaper distant one on total cost.
Tailored sourcing portfolio: One globally cheapest supplier is best for every item, because unit price is the only sourcing dimension that reaches the income statement.

paper.caselet: A student can state what Seasonal relatives is, and now has to say why it changes the next decision.
paper.stem: Which explanation best connects Seasonal relatives to the wider subject?
options: Once Seasonal relatives has settled the choice, later evidence should not be allowed to reopen it, because a decision that keeps moving is not really a decision.
Separating the seasonal effect from the level is what lets a trend be estimated honestly and then put back in at the right size.
Seasonal relatives works in exactly the same way independently of the people, the constraints, and the decisions that surround it.
Seasonal relatives improves one local measure, so whatever happens elsewhere in the connected system can be treated as somebody else's problem to solve later on.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Newsvendor decision?
options: Newsvendor decision: Only the purchase cost of the item matters here, because salvage value and lost margin sit outside the ordering decision altogether.
Newsvendor decision: It assumes demand is constant and replenishment repeats indefinitely, so the same quantity is reordered in every cycle of the year.
Newsvendor decision: Underage and overage costs push the order quantity in the same direction, so raising either of them raises the quantity that should be ordered this season.
Newsvendor decision: The newsvendor model chooses a one-time quantity under uncertain demand by balancing the cost of one unit too few against one unit too many.

paper.caselet: A location model returns several stockyard configurations whose monthly totals fall between about ₹8.5 and ₹8.75 lakhs. One configuration requires two new sites; another uses one site that already operates and one new one.
paper.stem: How should the recommendation be made?
options: Rank the configurations by cost and take the lowest, since that is what the model was built to identify.
Treat differences inside that band as noise at the available data accuracy and choose on managerial practicality.
Re-run the model with tighter data, because a recommendation cannot rest on differences this small.
Choose the configuration with the most sites, since more stocking points always shorten the secondary distance travelled.

paper.stem: Which statement best explains Inventory functions and measures?
options: Inventory functions and measures: A higher inventory turnover is better without limit, because stock that moves faster cannot be stock that was needed and missing, so the line with the highest turns anywhere in the catalogue is by definition the best managed one.

Inventory functions and measures: The inventory functions run from meeting anticipated demand and smoothing production to decoupling operations, covering stockout risk and taking order-cycle economies, and the stock is read through inventory turnover and days of inventory.

Inventory functions and measures: Days of inventory and inventory turnover measure different things, so a firm can raise one without the other moving at all, and a report showing turns rising while days of inventory also rise needs no further explanation from the planner who produced it.

Inventory functions and measures: Cycle inventory exists to protect against demand spikes and supply delays, while safety inventory is what ordering in batches leaves behind between deliveries, so a firm facing steadier demand should hold more cycle stock and less safety stock than one facing volatile demand.

paper.stem: Distinguish the paired frameworks: assign each claim or action to the correct row.
rows: Ecosystem actors and shipper decisions — principle
Ecosystem actors and shipper decisions — decision
choices: The macro ecosystem actors are shippers, the industry, infrastructure and service providers, and government, and shipper decision horizons sort a brand owner's choices into strategic, tactical and operational bands.
Read this at the industry level, where firms with similar attributes can act together on something none of them can move alone.
Map the full flow, expose waiting and indirect costs, segment service needs, and redesign the connected process rather than one function.
Re-engineering redesigns end-to-end flows to remove hidden time, inventory, hand-offs, and cost while meeting distinct customer service needs.

paper.stem: For each row, choose the precise explanation or action governed by that framework.
rows: Features of a good forecast — principle
Demand components and forecast error — principle
Features of a good forecast — decision
Demand components and forecast error — decision
choices: Every forecast assumes the past system continues, is never exact, is more accurate for groups than single items, and loses accuracy as the horizon lengthens — so it must be timely, stated with its error, and shared.
Read the near-zero bias as errors that cancel, and use mean absolute percentage error rather than mean absolute deviation when comparing this item against one selling in very different volumes.
Match the horizon to the decision's lead time, and accept the lower accuracy a two-month view carries rather than planning capacity from a number that arrives too late to act on.

Demand splits into a systematic component — level, trend, seasonality and cyclical movement — plus random variation, and the residual error is summarised as bias, mean absolute deviation and mean absolute percentage error.

paper.stem: Pair each framework label with the principle or decision that belongs to it.
choices: The three decision phases are supply chain design, supply chain planning and supply chain operations, separated by how long each commitment lasts and how much uncertainty is left when it is made.
Ask whether the decision widens customer value against total chain cost, since the margin any single stage reports never settles it.
Handle it as supply chain planning: hold the network fixed and set inventory, production and subcontracting policies across the horizon, because the design questions were already answered.

Supply chain surplus is customer value minus the total supply chain cost, and the customer is the single source of revenue, so every payment between firms only moves money the customer already paid in.
